items.streamTitle: Reducing polarization did not reduce false-news sharing—but an accuracy prompt helped
items.streamSummary: A randomized experiment separately changed feelings toward the opposing political party and made accuracy salient before a news-sharing task. Improving out-party affect did not measurably improve participants’ ability to distinguish true from false stories when deciding what to share, while the accuracy prompt did. The finding challenges the assumption that reducing affective polarization will automatically reduce misinformation sharing. The outcome was sharing intention in an experimental setting, not observed platform behavior.

items.streamTitle: FCMs can search backward from an objective to candidate changes
items.streamSummary: CF-BP adds an inverse capability to Fuzzy Cognitive Maps: rather than only asking what follows from a change, it searches for minimal modeled input changes that would move a target outcome. The peer-reviewed method uses analytical gradients and performed well against several counterfactual baselines. That can be valuable for decision support, but “causally consistent” here means consistent with the relationships encoded in the FCM; it does not prove those relationships are causally correct in the real world.
items.attribution: Tyrovolas, Nápoles & Stylios — IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics

items.streamTitle: NATO StratCom is bringing synthetic audiences into live training
items.streamSummary: SYNESIS 2026 will combine AI-enabled agents, real-time simulation, and Audience Behaviour Modelling in a NATO StratCom COE live exercise focused on hostile information influence and hybrid threats. The development matters because synthetic audiences are moving into operationally relevant training rather than remaining academic demos. What is not yet public is equally important: there is no demonstrated evidence that the simulated audience responses predict how real people would respond.

items.streamTitle: Taiwan’s election warning turns “cognitive warfare” into observable conduct categories
items.streamSummary: Taiwan’s governing DPP China Affairs Department published a set of concrete election-interference behaviors it says can trigger legal consequences, including directed travel, benefits for political support, foreign-funded polling or propaganda, intermediaries, and intelligence-related activity. The useful analytical move is from an umbrella label to observable conduct and evidence artifacts. Because the warning comes from a political actor with direct electoral interests, it should be read as a defensive threat model rather than proof of how prevalent or effective each tactic is.
items.attribution: Taipei Times / DPP China Affairs Department

items.streamTitle: Synthetic respondents can sound diverse while being statistically repetitive
items.streamSummary: A psychometric validation study found that GPT-generated survey respondents used less of the response range, repeated patterns more often, and occupied a narrower multivariate space than a human reference sample. More than 5% of synthetic profiles gave the same response across all 42 items, compared with 0.7% of human profiles, even though the model’s free-text explanations sounded varied. The finding is model- and instrument-specific, but it shows why fluent prose is a poor substitute for distributional validation.

items.streamTitle: Use the LLM to operate the model—not to be the model
items.streamSummary: A crowd-management digital-twin prototype pairs a conversational Gemini interface with an explicit agent-based simulation engine. The simulator, not the LLM, governs movement, queues, occupancy, balking, and evacuation, while natural language is used to configure scenarios and inspect results. The architecture is attractive because it keeps behavioral rules auditable. The prototype reached technical scale in synthetic scenarios, but it has not yet demonstrated real-time calibration or predictive validity against actual crowd events.

items.streamTitle: Acknowledgment can create common ground without requiring agreement
items.streamSummary: In a preregistered randomized study of 558 U.S. adults, messages that affirmed either an opposing viewpoint’s arguments or its intentions improved perceived perspective-taking, fairness, similarity, common ground, and anticipated relationship quality. The finding suggests that acknowledgment can improve the relational conditions for disagreement without requiring agreement. These are immediate relational outcomes, however, not evidence of durable persuasion or long-term behavior change.

items.streamTitle: Calling symptoms “normal” can unintentionally signal that treatment is unnecessary
items.streamSummary: Across 14 studies involving 9,371 participants, reassurance that described symptoms as “normal” reduced reported willingness to seek treatment. The effect was not explained only by reduced anxiety: participants inferred an implicit treatment norm, as though “normal” also meant “you do not need to act.” The work is a strong example of unintended pragmatic inference and shows why communicators should distinguish prevalence from recommended action. The studies were largely online, so real clinical behavior still needs field validation.

items.streamTitle: Social influence becomes clearer when you specify who, where, how, and which behavior
items.streamSummary: A Nature Climate Change perspective proposes a four-part way to unpack social influence: who is influencing, where influence is directed, how influence occurs, and which behavior is targeted. The value is less a new psychological effect than a disciplined schema for comparing interventions and evidence. It prevents “influence” from being used simultaneously as actor, method, mechanism, and outcome. The framework comes from climate-action research, so specific interaction effects still need testing in other settings.
items.attribution: Hampton, Latter & Whitmarsh — Nature Climate Change

items.streamTitle: Double Machine Learning offers a path from expert FCM edges to empirical estimates
items.streamSummary: A causal-mapping preprint treats each stakeholder-defined FCM edge as a treatment–outcome hypothesis and estimates selected edge strengths from longitudinal data with Double Machine Learning. Synthetic tests and a real socio-environmental application show how expert topology and data-driven estimation can coexist. The method is promising because it differs from simply optimizing weights for predictive fit, but it remains a preprint and still depends on confounding, measurement, temporal-ordering, and graph-validity assumptions.

items.streamTitle: NATO is institutionalizing cognitive resilience—but measurement still lags
items.streamSummary: NATO Defense College’s 2026 Conference of Commandants brought together 108 participants from 67 defense institutions around cognitive warfare and resilience. The official synthesis shows the concept moving into professional education, defense planning, and capability development, with emphasis on biases, emotion, trust, and decision-making. What remains unclear is effectiveness: the event documents institutional adoption, not whether particular curricula measurably improve decisions under manipulation or uncertainty. The next step is turning “resilience” into specific trainable and testable capabilities.

items.streamTitle: Changing the feed changed exposure and norm perception—but not users’ own engagement behavior
items.streamSummary: An eight-week randomized feed experiment around the 2024 U.S. election found that engagement-based ranking increased exposure to moralized, intergroup, emotional, and toxic political content and reduced the accuracy of users’ perceptions of social norms. A diversified feed improved norm accuracy while preserving enjoyment. Yet the ranking intervention did not significantly change users’ own engagement behavior. The result is a useful reminder that exposure, social perception, and behavior can move independently even inside the same causal experiment.

items.streamTitle: Behavioral experiments can provide the thresholds used in diffusion models
items.streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study estimated individual adoption thresholds from behavioral choice experiments and then used those thresholds inside network-diffusion simulations. The simulations showed that strategies based only on network position can be suboptimal when people differ in how much social exposure they need before adopting. The contribution is methodological: it links measured micro-level behavior to agent parameters instead of inventing universal thresholds. How well the approach transfers depends on the behavior, population, and network being modeled.
items.attribution: Tănase, Algesheimer & Mariani — Nature Human Behaviour

items.streamTitle: News trust fell while use of the trusted source increased
items.streamSummary: A field experiment with readers of Süddeutsche Zeitung warned about the difficulty of distinguishing real from AI-generated images. Concern about misinformation rose and reported trust in news fell, including trust in the newspaper itself. Yet readers visited the outlet more afterward and subscriber retention was higher five months later. The result shows why survey attitudes and revealed behavior should be measured separately: a warning can make the information environment feel less trustworthy while increasing the relative value of a source people already rely on.

items.streamTitle: A causal digital twin asks who benefits from the intervention—not just who is at risk
items.streamSummary: DINIRS combines patient-state modeling with doubly robust causal estimation to predict how different patients might respond to alternative respiratory-support strategies. External validation strengthened the proof of concept, but the individual counterfactual effects remain observational estimates and the authors call for prospective testing. The broader lesson is useful beyond medicine: decision support should distinguish predicting an outcome from estimating how an intervention changes that outcome for different people.

items.streamTitle: A realistic synthetic population is not automatically a valid synthetic human
items.streamSummary: Animarium released a deterministic pipeline that builds more than 1.8 million synthetic people and 887,000 households for 11 Italian municipalities from public demographic and survey data. The project tracks provenance and distinguishes empirically constrained attributes from generated biographies, while explicitly declining to claim behavioral validity. That separation is valuable for synthetic-audience work: a population can be statistically plausible and reproducible without proving that generated agents will respond like real people.

items.streamTitle: AI permission policies reduced prompts but made overreach protection worse
items.streamSummary: In a controlled study, reusable user-written permission rules reduced how often an AI agent had to ask for approval, but they also blocked less overreach than per-action human approval or automated review. Most overreach that still occurred under the policy condition followed an explicit human approval in context. The result highlights a behavioral governance problem: stated standing preferences are not always durable commitments when convenience, urgency, or trust enters the moment of action.

items.streamTitle: True content can still create a false inference
items.streamSummary: RCMN reframes misleadingness as a relationship between a message, its evidence, and the interpretation a reader is likely to draw. Its dataset includes unsupported inference, exaggeration, omission, arousal, and intent rather than treating misinformation as fabrication alone. Foundation models often recovered likely interpretations more easily than the actual misleading mechanism. The framework is still a preprint, but it offers a useful analytical reminder: factual accuracy and audience interpretation are not the same variable.

items.streamTitle: Cleaning a survey can make the sample more biased
items.streamSummary: Pew tested several ways to remove bogus respondents from an online opt-in survey of more than 11,000 U.S. adults. Trap questions and prescreening improved multiple quality indicators, but voter-file matching sometimes removed legitimate people who were harder to identify while retaining some bogus respondents, and all screening approaches shifted substantive estimates. The practical lesson is that “cleaning” data is not neutral: screening can create selection bias that matters for audience analysis and model calibration.

items.streamTitle: Sensors are not states—and states are not mission effects
items.streamSummary: An ARES 2026 cyber-defense model separates three layers that are often collapsed: observed telemetry, inferred adversary/system state, and mission-level risk. Bayesian updates feed a higher-level decision model that weighs residual risk against action cost, with robustness checks under noisy telemetry. The specific cyber model is domain-bound, but the architecture is broadly useful for decision support because it makes uncertainty and abstraction explicit instead of treating an indicator as the underlying condition.

items.streamTitle: Visible messages can miss the state changes happening inside an influence network
items.streamSummary: A controlled LLM-agent benchmark found that direct exposure reliably shifted later probed stances, peer relays carried smaller effects, and the agents’ visible messages did not always reveal the stance changes measured internally. The agents are not validated substitutes for humans, so this is not evidence of human persuasion dynamics. Its value is methodological: influence measurement should preserve who saw what, through whom, what state changed, and what action followed instead of treating content volume as the effect.

items.streamTitle: AI-generated election prebunks moved from experiment to a reusable tool
items.streamSummary: A preregistered panel experiment with 4,293 U.S. voters found that LLM-generated prebunking articles reduced belief in election rumors and modestly protected confidence in election administration, with smaller effects still visible a week later. Once researchers had refined the underlying template, fully AI-generated messages performed comparably to versions receiving per-rumor human feedback. The work shows how validated behavioral design can be front-loaded before automation, although the outcomes were self-reported beliefs rather than field behavior.
